```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Idea

The aim of this model is to predict the Premier League ranking of teams at the end of the season. To do this I will predict the goals scored in each match of the given fixture, convert this into predicted points, add these points up, to then get a final ranking that orders the team with respect to:

1.  Total number of points at the end of the season
2.  Goal difference at the end of the season. (also keep track of GF and GA)

## Model building

Firstly, I want to visualize the possible variables that might be used to model our prediction.

```{r}
goal_data <- data.frame(Goals = c(train_data$FTHG, train_data$FTAG))

ggplot(goal_data, aes(x = Goals)) + geom_bar() + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:max(goal_data$Goals, na.rm = TRUE)) +labs(title = "Goals scored per match",x = "Goals",y = "Number of team performances") + theme_minimal()
```

This shows how often each score occurred. It’s a useful first look, but the overall goal distribution alone can’t tell you whether a Poisson model fits well once predictors are included. (HERE ADD THAT WE USE POISSON BECAUSE IS THE DISTRIBTION OF COUNTS!!!!!!)

## Model selection using stepwise method selection and AIC

The model predicts the number of goals scored by the home team and the number scored by the away team. It uses statistics from previous matches as inputs. The current match’s final result and statistics are not used as inputs, because that information would not be available before the match.

Now we look at a stepwise method selection to choose the model with lowest AIC.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
predictor_columns <- c("HomeFTGoalsBefore", "AwayFTGoalsBefore", "HTPB", "ATPB", "HomeShotsBefore", "AwayShotsBefore", "HomeShotsOnTargetBefore", "AwayShotsOnTargetBefore", "HomeCornersBefore", "AwayCornersBefore", "HomeFoulsBefore", "AwayFoulsBefore", "HomeYellowCardsBefore", "AwayYellowCardsBefore", "HomeRedCardsBefore", "AwayRedCardsBefore")

#variables we will use in our models (i.e. predict (FTHG and FTAG) and use predictor_columns)
home_train <- train_data[, c("FTHG", predictor_columns)] 
away_train <- train_data[, c("FTAG", predictor_columns)]

#full model formulas
home_full_formula <- reformulate(predictor_columns, response = "FTHG") #FTHG ~ sum(predictor_columns) 
away_full_formula <- reformulate(predictor_columns, response = "FTAG")

#null models
home_null <- glm(FTHG ~ 1, data = home_train, family = poisson)
away_null <- glm(FTAG ~ 1, data = away_train, family = poisson)

#full models
home_full <- glm(home_full_formula, data = home_train, family = poisson)
away_full <- glm(away_full_formula, data = away_train, family = poisson)

#forward backward selection using AIC
home_step <- step(home_null, scope = list(lower = ~1, upper = home_full_formula), direction = "both")
away_step <- step(away_null, scope = list(lower = ~1, upper = away_full_formula), direction = "both")

# comparison
AIC(home_null, home_step, home_full)
AIC(away_null, away_step, away_full)

```

For each response, the lowest AIC is the best of the models compared by that criterion. The forward-backward models selected by AIC are:

```{r}
formula(home_step)
formula(away_step)
```

## Checking the selected models

Now, since we're applying a glm, we want to look at the residual plots for glms.

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(home_step)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(away_step)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Poisson goals are discrete counts, so their residuals aren’t expected to look like normally distributed residuals. To check whether using this model makes sense we can check the Pearson residuals, which help us check for overdispersion:

```{r}
c(Home = sum(residuals(home_step, type = "pearson")^2) /df.residual(home_step),
  Away = sum(residuals(away_step, type = "pearson")^2) /df.residual(away_step))
```

Since the Pearson dispersion ratios are close to 1, there is no strong sign of overdispersion as a ratio near 1 is expected for a well-fitting Poisson model.

## Predicting c(Goals scored, goals conceded, points) for each team

### Checking teams

```{r}
train_teams<-unique(c(train_data$HomeTeam, train_data$AwayTeam))
length(train_teams)
length(intersect(train_teams, unique(c(test_data$HomeTeam, test_data$AwayTeam))))
```

This tells us that from the train data set we have all the teams data from our test set which is great as this gives us more information for all of our observations.

```{r}
length(intersect(train_teams, unique(c(prediction_data$HomeTeam, prediction_data$AwayTeam))))
setdiff(unique(c(prediction_data$HomeTeam, prediction_data$AwayTeam)),train_teams)
```

On the other hand, for our prediction dataset we do not have information for all the teams. This means that we won't have that much information for `Coventry` as the only information that we have is the first three months of the 2026/27 premier league season. This will then be expanded in our Limitations section.

### Model Fitting

Now we fit our selected models.

```{r}
text_columns <- names(train_data)[sapply(train_data, is.character)] #names the text columns in the dataset
train_data[text_columns] <- lapply(train_data[text_columns], factor) #applies factor() to the text columns
test_data[text_columns] <- lapply(test_data[text_columns], factor) #applies factor() to the text columns

#predict goals for each match in the test season
test_data$PredHomeGoals <- round(predict(home_step, newdata = test_data, type = "response")) #using home model
test_data$PredAwayGoals <- round(predict(away_step, newdata = test_data, type = "response")) #using away model
```

We want to create a table of all of our predictions to then order these wrt points (and add a goal difference condition too). This function turns a set of match predictions into a rank:

```{r}
ranking <- function(matches, home_goals, away_goals) {
  #home rank
  home_points <-ifelse(home_goals > away_goals, 3, ifelse(home_goals == away_goals, 1, 0))
  home_ranking <- data.frame(Team = matches$HomeTeam, Points = home_points, GF = home_goals, GA = away_goals)
  #away rank
  away_points <- ifelse(away_goals > home_goals,3, ifelse(away_goals == home_goals, 1, 0))
  away_ranking <- data.frame(Team = matches$AwayTeam, Points = away_points, GF = away_goals, GA = home_goals)

  all_team_matches <- rbind(home_ranking, away_ranking)

  final_ranking <- aggregate(cbind(Points, GF, GA) ~ Team, data = all_team_matches, sum) #cbind(Points, GF, GA) combines those three columns as the response and ~ Team says to group the rows by Team. sum is the function applied to each column within each team’s group

  final_ranking$GD <- final_ranking$GF - final_ranking$GA #create new goal difference column for each team 
  
  #ordering
  final_ranking <- final_ranking[order(-final_ranking$Points, -final_ranking$GD), ] #order() uses GD to break ties in Points, so teams with the same points are ordered by highest goal difference first
  final_ranking$Position <- seq_len(nrow(final_ranking)) #adding a column that tells us the position

  final_ranking <- final_ranking[c("Position", "Team", "Points", "GD")]
  rownames(final_ranking) <- NULL

  final_ranking
}
```

Now we apply our predicted goals to test our model.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
predicted_table <- ranking(test_data, test_data$PredHomeGoals, test_data$PredAwayGoals)
predicted_table
```

Now we want to compare our prediction to the actual results. First we make the table with the actual results and then we merge the prediction and actual.

```{r}
actual_table <- ranking(test_data, test_data$FTHG, test_data$FTAG)

table_comparison <- merge(predicted_table, actual_table, by = "Team", suffixes = c("_Predicted", "_Actual"))
table_comparison$PositionDifference <- table_comparison$Position_Predicted - table_comparison$Position_Actual
table_comparison <- table_comparison[order(table_comparison$Position_Actual),] #order wrt actual position

table_comparison
```

## 2026/27 season prediction

I will use the actual results for 2026/27 matches that have already been played and predict the remaining fixtures. The `prediction_data` has results for up to 19-10-26 and the remaining rows are filled with `NA` so we want to predict the remaining rows. We do so following a similar structure as we did before.

```{r}
played_26_27 <- prediction_data[prediction_data$Date <= as.Date("2026-10-19"),] 
unplayed <- prediction_data$Date > as.Date("2026-10-19")

final_train_data <- bind_rows(train_data, test_data, played_26_27) #known data that will get used to train the model

home_final_model <- glm(formula(home_step), data = final_train_data, family = poisson) 
away_final_model <- glm(formula(away_step), data = final_train_data, family = poisson)

#initialise prediction column filled with NAs
prediction_data$PredHomeGoals <- NA_real_ 
prediction_data$PredAwayGoals <- NA_real_

prediction_data$PredHomeGoals[unplayed] <- predict(home_final_model, newdata = prediction_data[unplayed, ], type = "response")
prediction_data$PredAwayGoals[unplayed] <- predict(away_final_model, newdata = prediction_data[unplayed, ], type = "response")

final_home_goals <- ifelse(unplayed,prediction_data$PredHomeGoals,prediction_data$FTHG) 
final_away_goals <- ifelse(unplayed,prediction_data$PredAwayGoals,prediction_data$FTAG)

#builds the prediction table
predicted_2026_27_table <- ranking(prediction_data,final_home_goals,final_away_goals)

predicted_2026_27_table
```

Notice, we have that Manchester City is likely to end up as the winner of the season. However, due to legal reasons, there is a popular thought that this team will get relegated. Hence, it's worth having a look at what the result would be without this team. In the following code chunck there is a data cleaning function which reoves all of th erows containing either Home Team = Man City or Away Team = Man City. This chunck should be copied at the start of this file to produce a prediction excluding Man City from prediction. Note that it's necessary to keep the Man City observations from past datasets.

```{r}
#prediction_data <- prediction_data[prediction_data$HomeTeam != "Man City" & prediction_data$AwayTeam != "Man City", ]
```

Note: the model only predicts home and away goals for each match (so not each variable that we used at the beginning to train the model). Notcice that with the `2026/27` data that we have, we already have an initial performance of every team for this season. However, the glm doesn't give greater weight to more recent observations which might be important for this model given that there are some teams whose data is minimal. To add a weight to a glm in R we can use `glm(formula(home_step), data = final_train_data, family = poisson, weights = ))` and find a formula that gives greater weight to more recent observations.
